research_question: In people with patellofemoral pain syndrome, what is the short-term effect (up to 3 months) of exercise therapy versus no treatment, placebo, waiting list, health educational material, or—when exercise is added to a co-intervention—the same co-intervention alone, on functional ability measured with knee-function questionnaires?
treatment_label: Exercise therapy, alone or added to a co-intervention
control_label: No treatment, placebo, waiting list, health educational material, or the same co-intervention without exercise
outcome_description: Short-term functional ability assessed up to 3 months after randomization or treatment initiation using a validated knee-function questionnaire (e.g., Anterior Knee Pain Scale [AKPS]/Kujala score, Functional Index Questionnaire [FIQ], WOMAC function, or Lysholm score). If multiple eligible function measures are reported at the same time point, use AKPS/Kujala preferentially; otherwise apply a prespecified hierarchy of FIQ, WOMAC function, Lysholm, then another validated knee-function questionnaire. Orient all scales so higher harmonized values represent better function. Where multiple eligible assessments occur within 3 months, preferentially use the assessment closest to 3 months while avoiding duplicate inclusion of the same participants in a pooled estimate.
positive_direction: A positive Hedges g means that exercise therapy produces better short-term functional ability than the control condition.
search_queries: patellofemoral pain exercise therapy controlled trial functional ability
patellofemoral pain syndrome exercise rehabilitation trial knee function questionnaire
anterior knee pain exercise treatment comparison Kujala function outcome
inclusion_criteria: Original empirical studies of people with patellofemoral pain syndrome or clinically equivalent patellofemoral/anterior knee pain populations that evaluate exercise therapy, either alone or added to another intervention.
Studies with an eligible control condition: no treatment, placebo, waiting list, health educational material, or the same co-intervention without exercise.
Studies reporting a quantitative knee-related functional-ability outcome at an eligible short-term assessment up to 3 months, with sufficient information to calculate or recover an effect size.
exclusion_criteria: Not an original empirical study; systematic reviews, meta-analyses, editorials, opinion pieces, protocols without results, and theoretical papers are excluded.
No comparison between an exercise-therapy treatment condition and an eligible control condition, including failure to hold a co-intervention constant when estimating the added effect of exercise.

No quantitative outcome data capable of producing an effect size; eligible information includes means and SDs, change-score data, t/F-values, proportions, odds ratios, or other convertible statistics obtainable from authors.
Completely unrelated to patellofemoral pain syndrome, exercise therapy, or knee-related functional ability.
moderators_to_extract: Exercise modality and content (e.g., hip-focused, knee-focused, combined, supervised/home-based)
Exercise dose and treatment duration (frequency, intensity, session length, and total weeks)
Comparator type (no treatment, placebo, waiting list, education, or matched co-intervention)
Timing of functional assessment within the 0-to-3-month window
Functional questionnaire used (AKPS/Kujala, FIQ, WOMAC, Lysholm, or other)
Participant and study characteristics (age, sex distribution, symptom duration, baseline severity, and randomized versus nonrandomized design)
effect_size_note: For continuous functional-ability outcomes, calculate small-sample-corrected standardized mean differences (Hedges g), using post-intervention values when available and otherwise compatible change scores, and reverse-score instruments such as WOMAC variants when necessary so positive effects consistently favor exercise. Prefer AKPS/Kujala when multiple eligible function questionnaires are reported, and select the assessment closest to 3 months when several eligible short-term time points are available. For multi-arm studies, avoid double-counting shared controls by combining eligible exercise arms when clinically appropriate or splitting the shared control; estimate the added effect of exercise only from contrasts in which co-interventions are balanced. Pool with a random-effects model, report 95% confidence and prediction intervals, quantify heterogeneity with tau-squared and I-squared, assess risk of bias using an appropriate design-specific tool, and examine small-study effects when enough studies are available.
